system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2124-02-10 14:07:00 to 2124-02-12 14:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a two-week history of nonproductive cough and shortness of breath. A chest X-ray revealed left lower lobe pneumonia, and she was started on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin, with oxygen support initially at 2 liters per minute. Her oxygen needs improved within 1.5 days, and she was weaned to room air. She remained stable throughout the admission, with normal blood pressure and kidney function. Her home medications for hypertension, diastolic heart failure, and hyperlipidemia were continued. She was discharged home on oral antibiotics, including cefpodoxime and azithromycin, with adjustments to her furosemide dosing and instructions to follow a 2-gram sodium diet and monitor daily weight. Follow-up was arranged with her primary care provider.

radiology_notes.text:
SINGLE VIEW OF THE CHEST:  

HISTORY:  ___ woman with cough, fever, shortness of breath and
hypoxia.  Assess for infiltrate.

COMPARISON:  A series of chest x-rays, most recently ___ dating back to
___.

FINDINGS:  A single portable semi-upright AP view of the chest was obtained.
Lung volumes are low.  Cardiomegaly and tortuosity of the aorta are stable. No
airspace consolidation or large effusion is identified, although the
retrocardiac area is difficult to assess on this frontal view.

Bilateral nodular pleural thickening is stable.  There are stable degenerative
changes of the shoulder.

IMPRESSION:  Limited single view study without acute intrathoracic process.
Please refer to CT chest performed concurrently.

TWO-VIEW STUDY OF THE CHEST

HISTORY:  ___ woman with shortness of breath, difficult portable chest
x-ray to evaluate.  Please evaluate for infiltrate.

COMPARISON:  Portable chest x-ray from today (___) at 8:54 a.m., a series
of chest x-rays from ___ through ___ and CTA of the chest,
___.

FINDINGS:  Frontal and lateral views of the chest were obtained.  Lung volumes
are low.  There is no focal airspace consolidation.  The retrocardiac space is
clear. The cardiac silhouette is top normal in size. Areas of peripheral
pleural nodularity are unchanged. There is scoliosis of the thoracic spine and
degenerative change of the shoulders. 

IMPRESSION:  Low lung volumes.  No evidence of pneumonia. Please refer to CT
chest performed subsequently.

CTA OF THE CHEST WITHOUT AND WITH CONTRAST

HISTORY:  ___ female with initial hypoxia on arrival, no infiltrate on
chest x-ray.  Please evaluate for pulmonary embolism.

COMPARISON:  CTA of the chest ___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CTA images of the chest were obtained following
administration of intravenous contrast.  Prior to administration of contrast,
MDCT images of the chest were obtained.  Multiplanar reformatted images were
generated.

FINDINGS:  NON-CONTRAST CT OF THE CHEST:  There is no intramural hematoma.

CTA OF THE CHEST:  There are bilateral pulmonary emboli.  There are right
lobar, segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli of the right upper and
right lower lobes. Segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli also noted in
the left lower lobe.  These are best appreciated on images 3:34 and 3:52.
There is no evidence of right heart strain.

A right upper lobe nodule (3:40) measures 9 x 6 mm, and is stable in
comparison to CTA chest ___.  Prevascular and hilar lymph nodes are
not pathologically enlarged by size criteria.  Foci of prominent extrapleural
fat are stable. Evaluation of the lung bases is limited by motion. Scattered
ground glass opacities in the lungs likely reflect expiratory phase and
hypoventilatory effects. 

The thoracic aorta is normal in caliber. Atheroma is noted in the aorta at the
level of the diaphragm.

There is a low-density lesion within the left lobe of the thyroid, not
completely imaged on this study but appears stable in comparison to ___.

Limited imaging through the upper abdomen demonstrates a small hiatal hernia.
There are mild degenerative changes of the thoracic spine.  No suspicious
lytic or blastic osseous lesion is identified.

IMPRESSION:

Bilateral pulmonary emboli involving branches of the right upper and right
lower lobes, and left lower lobe. No evidence of right heart strain. Findings
were posted to the Emergency Department dashboard following initial review.

conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ . You’re here because of chest pain and shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My chest pain on the left side has been worse for five days. It’s a burning, tight feeling. And I’ve been struggling to catch my breath, especially when I move or take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any cough, fever, or palpitations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a dry cough and felt feverish. Also, my heart has been racing sometimes, and I’ve felt dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We did a CT scan of your chest in the ER, and it showed blood clots in both lungs—what we call pulmonary emboli. That’s likely why you’re having these symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood clots in my lungs? That sounds serious. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we’ve started treatment. You’re on a blood thinner through your IV called heparin, and you’re getting oxygen to help you breathe easier. We’ll switch to other medications soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clots before in my leg. Is this related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of DVT—deep vein thrombosis—puts you at higher risk. We think that’s what led to these clots in your lungs. We’ll keep you on blood thinners to prevent more clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my chest pain and headache? They’ve been bad for a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’ve had chronic left-sided chest pain and headaches. The chest pain may feel worse now because of the clots. We’re giving you acetaminophen with codeine for pain, and we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also take ibuprofen at home. Can I keep using that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use ibuprofen if needed, but we’re being cautious because of your kidney function. We noticed your creatinine went up a bit, so we’re watching your kidneys closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys? What happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine rose to 1.3, up from your usual 0.7 or 0.8. This may be from the contrast dye used in the CT scan or from mild dehydration. We’ve given you IV fluids, and your levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So it’s getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last lab showed creatinine back down to 0.7. That’s a good sign. We’ll keep checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my heart? I have heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your beta blocker for heart failure. Your furosemide was paused because of the kidney issue, but we’ll restart it once we’re sure your kidneys are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on metoprolol. We’re keeping your blood pressure well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My breathing isn’t as bad, but I still need the oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ve switched you from heparin to a medication called Lovenox, which you’ll get as a shot twice a day. You’ll also start Coumadin, a pill that works over days to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of Coumadin. I need blood tests for that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We checked your INR today—it’s 1.7. We want it above 2. Until then, you’ll keep taking Lovenox along with Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll go home with both?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Lovenox shots for five more days and Coumadin. You’ll need a blood test soon after discharge to check your INR and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I send the results to?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To Dr. ___. The lab will fax them directly. He’ll adjust your Coumadin dose based on the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxygen? Do I need that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with oxygen at 2 liters. It’s a precaution while your lungs recover. We’ll reassess in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is stable, and your kidneys are back to normal. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lovenox shots twice daily for five days and take Coumadin as prescribed. Resume your usual medications, including furosemide, ibuprofen as needed, and your stomach protector, pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use acetaminophen-codeine as needed for pain, and ibuprofen if that’s not enough. But avoid NSAIDs if you feel unwell or have stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have worsening chest pain, trouble breathing, fever, or swelling in your legs, call your doctor or go to the ER right away. These could be signs of another clot or complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your home health team follows up. Take care, and follow those instructions closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your granddaughter can help you with the Lovenox shots if needed. The nurse will show her how before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s been helping me. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to be going home, but I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach. Recovery takes time, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get the blood test done right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. That’s very important for adjusting your Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up, and Dr. ___ will manage your anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well, and we’ll get you home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will review your medications and oxygen setup before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We want to make sure you’re safe and informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thank you again.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath over five days, found to have bilateral pulmonary emboli on CT angiography. She was treated with heparin initially, then transitioned to enoxaparin and warfarin. Her oxygen requirement improved, and she was discharged on home oxygen at 2 liters per minute. She developed transient acute kidney injury, likely contrast-induced, which resolved with IV fluids. Her heart failure and hypertension were managed with continued beta-blocker therapy and temporary hold of furosemide during renal impairment. Chronic pain was controlled with acetaminophen-codeine. She was discharged in stable condition with instructions to continue anticoagulation, monitor INR and creatinine, and follow up with her physician.
